extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, poets, and students of dramatic theory (writers of tragedy)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing tragic drama: construction of plot, character, and the poetic elements that produce pity and fear. Emphasises how to arrange incidents, recognitions, reversals, and the parts of a tragedy for maximal tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot as the first principle / imitation of an action
rubrics_metrics.description: The Plot is the first principle and the soul of a tragedy: Tragedy is the imitation of an action, and of the agents, mainly with a view to the action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plot must be a whole (complete and of a certain magnitude) with a beginning, middle, and end; it should imitate one action that is whole and complete. The plot, not a sequence of fine speeches or portraits, produces the essential tragic effect because key emotional elements (peripeteia and recognition) are parts of the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and structure of beginning, middle, end
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole is that which has a beginning (does not itself follow anything by causal necessity), a middle (follows something and is followed), and an end (naturally follows something and has nothing following it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A well-constructed plot must neither begin nor end at haphazard but conform to these principles so that the sequence of events is perspicuous and causally coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude / proper length
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy must be of a certain magnitude — large enough to be beautiful but small enough to be embraced in one view and by memory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If too small the view is confused; if too large unity is lost. The proper magnitude admits of a sequence of events that allow a change from bad fortune to good or from good to bad in accordance with probability or necessity. The limit as fixed by dramatic nature is that length should be easily embraced by memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of plot (single action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Unity of plot is not unity of hero but unity of the action: the plot must imitate one action so that if any part is displaced the whole is disjointed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An action is one when the structural union of parts is such that removal of any part disturbs the whole; incidents without necessary or probable connexion are not organic to the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causality / law of probability or necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Events in a tragedy should follow according to the law of probability or necessity rather than mere sequence of occurrences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry relates what may happen (the universal) rather than what has happened (the particular). Plots should show causal or probable connections (propter hoc not merely post hoc) so outcomes arise from preceding actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character as second principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Character holds the second place after plot: Character reveals moral purpose, showing what kind of things a man chooses or avoids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speeches that do not manifest choice or avoidance are not expressive of character. Well finished diction and precision of portraiture often precede plot-construction in novices, but character must serve the action rather than replace it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought as the third element
rubrics_metrics.description: Thought is the faculty of saying what is possible and pertinent in given circumstances; in oratory this corresponds to rhetoric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thought appears where something is proved or a general maxim is enunciated; it helps make characters speak the language appropriate to civic or rhetorical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction (expression in words) as the fourth element
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction is the expression of the meaning in words; its essence is the same in verse and prose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction concerns how meaning is rendered verbally and contributes to the poet's art, but is a subordinate element to plot, character, and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song and spectacle as embellishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Song holds the chief place among embellishments; the Spectacle has emotional attraction but is the least artistic part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spectacular effects depend more on stage machinery than the poet's art. While spectacle can attract, the power of tragedy is felt even without representation and actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of episodic (epeisodic) plots
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'epeisodic' plot is one in which episodes or acts succeed one another without probable or necessary sequence; such plots are the worst.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bad poets compose episodic works by fault; good poets sometimes do so to please players or competitions, stretching plot beyond natural continuity. The plot must not be a mere series of loosely connected episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use surprise with causal connection
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic effect is best produced when events come by surprise and when they follow as cause and effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprising events that nevertheless have an air of design produce greater tragic wonder than mere coincidence; examples like the statue of Myron falling on a murderer illustrate striking but apparently designed coincidences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs Complex plots
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots are Simple (one continuous action without Reversal or Recognition) or Complex (change involves Reversal and/or Recognition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex plots that contain properly arising reversals and recognitions from the plot's internal structure are superior; simplicity lacks those producing the strongest tragic emotions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripeteia (Reversal of Intention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversal of Intention is a change by which the action veers round to its opposite, subject to probability or necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reversals should arise naturally from the plot (e.g., a messenger intending to comfort instead causes opposite effect). Reversal is one of the main mechanisms producing pity and fear when properly integrated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anagnorisis (Recognition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognition is a change from ignorance to knowledge, producing love or hate between persons destined for good or bad fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The best recognition is coincident with a Reversal of Intention (as in Oedipus). Recognitions can be of persons or of facts, and may involve trivial objects; they should be intimately bound to the plot and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic incident (painful or destructive action)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Tragic Incident is a destructive or painful action (death on stage, bodily agony, wounds, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragic incidents are part of the situations producing pity and fear; they are elements of the whole and should be treated as such in construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative parts of tragedy (prologue, episode, exodos, choric song)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy is divided into quantitative parts: Prologue (part preceding Parodos), Episode (parts between complete choric songs), Exodos (part without a choric song after it); Choric parts include Parodos, Stasimon, Commos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions: Parodos = first chorus utterance; Stasimon = choric ode without anapaests or trochaic tetrameters; Commos = joint lamentation of chorus and actors. These parts are common structural elements that must be organized as elements of the whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim at actions that excite pity and fear
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect tragedy should imitate actions which excite pity and fear; this is the distinctive mark of tragic imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The change of fortune presented must not be the spectacle of a virtuous man brought from prosperity to adversity (this shocks but moves neither pity nor fear), nor of a bad man passing to prosperity, nor the downfall of an utter villain. Rather the protagonist should be a man 'not eminently good and just, yet whose misfortune is brought about not by vice but by some error or frailty.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of character (medium between extremes)
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic protagonist should be a character between moral extremes — not eminently good nor totally villainous — whose downfall arises from error or frailty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a character (e.g., Oedipus, Thyestes) is highly renowned and prosperous, and his misfortune through error arouses pity and fear. The protagonist's misfortune must be unmerited or not wholly deserved so pity can be elicited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single issue preferred; change from good to bad
rubrics_metrics.description: A well-constructed plot should be single in its issue rather than double; the change of fortune should be from good to bad, not from bad to good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-issue tragedies (one decisive catastrophe) are artistically preferable; double-thread plots that end oppositely for good and bad are better suited to weaker spectator tastes and not the true tragic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition that plot is primary over versification
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet/maker should be the maker of plots rather than of verses: the poet imitates actions and becomes such by the making of plots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when using historical subject matter, the poet is still maker if events conform to the laws of the probable and possible; names need not be traditional or famous so long as the constructed action is credible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversals and recognitions should arise from the plot's internal structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversals and Recognitions must arise from the internal structure of the plot so that consequences follow necessarily or probably from preceding actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These features should not be arbitrary devices but outcomes that the plot's organization makes natural, thereby producing genuine pity and fear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragic construction: avoid spectacle-substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not substitute spectacular effects for the poet's art; spectacular elements are less artistic and should not be relied upon to produce tragic power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The poet's art must produce tragic power even apart from actors and scenery; spectacle is the province of the stage machinist and is secondary to plot, character, thought, and diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer complex (worked-out) tragedy for maximal effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A perfect tragedy should, as we have seen, be arranged not on the simple but on the complex plan: complex plots (with recognition and reversal) better produce pity and fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practice of the stage bears out that well-worked complex plays are the most tragic in effect; the best tragedies are founded on stories of a few houses and illustrious families where errors produce catastrophic reversal.
